STATE OF NEW JERSEY
BEFORE THE PUBLIC EMPLOYMENT RELATIONS COMMISSION
In the Matter of
ELIZABETH BOARD OF EDUCATION
Respondent,
-and- Docket No. CI-2026-032
NEW JERSEY EDUCATION ASSOCIATION
Respondent,
-and-
VICTORIA WHITE,
Charging Party.
SYNOPSIS
The Public Employment Relations Commission affirms the
Director of Unfair Practices' dismissal of unfair practice
charges, alleging that the Board and the Association violated
N.J.S.A. 34:13A-1 5.4 a(1), (5) and 5.4b(1),(3), (7),
respectively of the Act. Regarding the charges against the
Board, the Commission finds that the Director properly dismissed
the a(5) charge because individual employees do not have standing
to pursue charges that the employer refused to negotiate in good
faith. The Commission further finds that the Director properly
dismissed the a(1) charge because of lack of subject matter
jurisdiction over the Charging Party's allegations of improper
payroll deductions from a back pay award obtained through a
tenure arbitration. Regarding the charges against the
Association, the Commission finds the Director properly dismissed
these clams, which amount to a breach of duty of representation
for the Association's alleged lack of assistance in filing
grievances regarding the payroll deduction issues. The Commission
concludes that given the discretion afforded to union in filing
grievances, the Charging Party did not establish that the
Association represented her in a manner that was arbitrary,
discriminatory, or in bad faith.
This synopsis is not part of the Commission decision. It
has been prepared for the convenience of the reader. It has been
neither reviewed nor approved by the Commission.

DECISION
On January 24, 2026, and later amended on February 3,
Victoria White (White or Charging Party) appealed from the
January 22 decision of the Director of Unfair Practices
(Director) refusing to issue a complaint and dismissing her
unfair practice charge (UPC or charge) filed against the
Elizabeth Board of Education (Board) and the New Jersey Education
Association (Association)(collectively Respondents).

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-41 2.
BACKGROUND
A. White’s UPCs
The original charge, filed on January 14, 2026, only
reproduced sections of the New Jersey Employer-Employee Relations
Act, N.J.S.A. 34:13A-1, et seq., with no further details. On
January 15, the Director notified White of several deficiencies
with the charge, and provided an extension until January 22 for
amendment. These deficiencies included: that the charge provide
a clear and concise statement of facts; establish that the claims
are within the 6-month statute of limitations; and proof of
service upon the Respondents.
On January 16, White amended her charge which included the
following sections:
(1) an 8-item section of “Facts”;
(2) a section titled “Unfair Practices by the Elizabeth
Board of Education”, alleging violation of 5.4a(1), (3), and
(5);
(3) a section titled “Unfair Practices by NJEA and EEA”,
alleging a violation of 5.4b(1); and
(4) a section titled “Relief Requested”, seeking that the
Board “cease and desist from deducting unemployment
compensation from my back-pay/arbitration award” and that
the Association “cease and desist from failing to fairly
represent me, to process my grievance properly, and to take
appropriate action to enforce the correct back-pay
calculation.”

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-41 3.
On January 21, White filed a second amendment to her charge
that stated the following, in pertinent part:1/
The Elizabeth Board of Education has
unlawfully deducted excessive amounts from my
December 23, 2025 paycheck (and prior
periods) for TPAF pension, pension loans,
NJEA dues, and unauthorized “unemployment
payments,” totaling $4,023.88 in deductions
from gross wages, leaving only $893.36 net-
nearly 100% withholding. Correct amounts are
TPAF pension $376.42, TPAF loan $380.71, NJEA
dues $75.00 (total $832.13); actual
deductions far exceed these, violating
multiple statutes.
Violations of N.J.S.A. 34:11-4.4 (Wage
Payment Law)
Exceeding authorized pension/loan amounts and
adding unapproved “unemployment” deductions
breaches subsection (a) (no unauthorized
diversions) and (d) (must be
reasonable/fair), as only law-mandated or
written-authorized withholdings are
permitted.
TPAF Statute Violations (N.J.S.A. 18A:66-35
et seq.)
Pension loan repayments cannot exceed 25% of
base salary per period (Division of Pensions
rule); doubling/tripling beyond $380.71
violates this cap and fixed contribution
rates ($376.42).
“Unemployment” has no TPAF basis.
Violations of N.J.S.A. 34:13A-5.4(a)
(Employer Prohibited Practices)

picture of a December 23, 2025 pay stub.

• (a)(5): Discrimination in employment terms
to discourage union membership, via targeted

2/ These provisions prohibit public employers, their
representatives or agents from: “(1) Interfering with,
restraining or coercing employees in the exercise of the
rights guaranteed to them by this act. . . .(5) Refusing to
negotiate in good faith with a majority representative of
employees in an appropriate unit concerning terms and
conditions of employment in that unit, or refusing to
process grievances presented by the majority
representative.”
3/ These provisions prohibit employee organizations, their
representatives or agents from: “(1) Interfering with,
restraining or coercing employees in the exercise of the
rights guaranteed to them by this act;” “(3) Refusing to
negotiate in good faith with a public employer, if they are
the majority representative of employees in an appropriate

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-41 5.

B. The Director’s Decision
By letter dated January 22, the Director dismissed both the
amended and second amended charges in their entirety, stating in
pertinent part:
Initially, please note that there is no
section 5.4b(7). If you were referring to
section 5.4a(7) or 5.4b(5), your allegations
are dismissed because the amended and second
amended charges allege a violation of same
without citing a NJ Public Employment
Relations Commission rule or regulation that
was violated. See City of Elizabeth, P.E.R.C.
No. 82-74, 8 NJPER 121 (¶13052 1982);
Palisades Park Bor., D.U.P. No. 78-1, 3 NJPER
238 (1977). Accordingly, any 5.4a(7) and
5.4b(5) allegations are hereby dismissed.
Your section 5.4a(5) and 5.4b(3) allegations
are dismissed because individual employees do
not have standing to pursue such claims; only
majority representatives and/or public
employers do. Section 5.4a(5) pertains to a
public employer refusing to negotiate in good
faith with a majority representative. Section
5.4b(3) pertains to a majority representative
refusing to negotiate in good faith with a
public employer. A public employer only has a
duty to your majority representative under
section 5.4a(5). A majority representative
only has a duty to your public employer under
section 5.4b(3). See New Jersey Turnpike
Auth. P.E.R.C. No. 81-64, 6 NJPER 560 (¶11284
1980) aff'd NJPER Supp.2d 101 (¶85 App. Div.

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-41 6.
1981); Union Cty. Ed. Services Comm’n and
Westlake Ed. Ass’n, D.U.P. 2000-13, 26 NJPER
160 (¶31062 2000).
Accordingly, your 5.4a(5) and 5.4b(3)
allegations are hereby dismissed.
Your section 5.4a(1), 5.4a(3), and 5.4b(1)
allegations are dismissed for the reasons set
forth in the letter dated January 15, 2026
and as set forth below.
Initially, the amended and second amended
charges do not provide a clear and concise
statement of the facts forming the basis of
your legal and factual claims against the
Respondent(s). See N.J.A.C. 19:14-1.3(a)(3).
A Respondent is entitled to know the
“particulars” of which it is charged. Town of
Westfield, P.E.R.C. No. 90-32, 15 NJPER 618
(¶20257 1989). Conclusory statements about a
Respondent's conduct does not satisfy our
pleading requirements. A charge should plead
with specificity the “who, what, when, where
and how” information about the commission of
an unfair practice in order to afford
Respondents adequate notice of the legal and
factual claims against them. State of New
Jersey (Judiciary), D.U.P. No. 2022-8, 48
NJPER 344 (¶77 2022); Edison Tp., D.U.P. No.
2012-9, 38 NJPER 269 (¶92 2012), aff’d
P.E.R.C. No. 2013-84, 40 NJPER 35 (¶14 2013);
Warren Cty. College, P.E.R.C. No. 2018-25, 44
NJPER 287 (¶80 2017).
With respect to the Statute of Limitations,
based upon what can be gleaned from your
charge “as is”, it is unclear who did what
AND when they did same. Accordingly, you have
failed to demonstrate that an alleged/viable
unfair practice may have been committed
within six months of when your original
charge was filed on January 14, 2026, and
therefore your allegations fall outside the
Commission's jurisdiction. Moreover, the
amended and second unfair practice charges

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-41 7.
fail to provide a sufficient basis to toll
the six-month statute of limitations
particularly in the absence of any
explanation regarding how/if you were
prevented from filing a timely charge. See
N.J.S.A. 34:13A-5.4(c). The New Jersey
Supreme Court has held that “every person is
presumed to know the law.” State v. Moran,
202 N.J.311, 315, 319-320 (2010) (citing
Barlow v. United States, 32 U.S. 404, 411
(1833) (noting “a common maxim, familiar to
all minds, that ignorance of the law will not
excuse any person, either civilly or
criminally”)).
With respect to Subject Matter Jurisdiction,
it appears that the Commission lacks same
over your allegations/claims. We have no
authority to address whether pension loan
amounts or deductions were properly processed
by a public employer, or whether unemployment
benefits should be deducted from a back pay
award. On the latter issue, you have
acknowledged that unemployment benefits
concerning/related to back pay for the
120-day suspension are governed by Title 18A
provisions governing tenure charge
proceedings. As such, these allegations arise
under the education laws and you may consider
filing a petition with the Commissioner of
Education. See N.J.S.A. 18A:6-9 (issues
“arising under the education laws” must be
adjudicated by the Commissioner of
Education). Moreover, any challenge to
payroll deductions should be presented to the
Department of Labor's Division of Wage and
Hour Compliance.
Finally, your 5.4b(1) allegations essentially
appear to be a duty of fair representation
(DFR) claim against NJEA (and/or their
affiliate). A majority representative owes a
DFR to all unit employees, regardless of
union membership. A breach of the DFR occurs
only when a majority representative's conduct
towards a unit employee is “arbitrary,
discriminatory or in bad faith.” Middlesex
Cty. and Middlesex Council #7 (Mackaronis),

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-41 8.
P.E.R.C. No. 81-62, 6 NJPER 555, 557 (¶11282
1981), aff’d App. Div. Docket No. A-1455-80.
Majority representatives have a broad range
of discretion the Commission will generally
defer to in how they choose to handle the
processing and/or settlement of grievances.
State of New Jersey (JJC) and CWA Local 1040
(Thorpe), D.U.P. No. 2012-8, 38 NJPER 248
(¶83 2011), aff'd P.E.R.C. No. 2013-29, 39
NJPER 205 (¶66 2012); State of New Jersey
(Kean University) and Council of NJ College
Locals (Roman), D.U.P. No. 2015-10, 41 NJPER
497 (¶154 2015), aff'd P.E.R.C. No. 2015-76,
42 NJPER 33 (¶8 2015). Mere negligence,
incompetence or mistakes by the majority
representative in the handling of grievances
at the hearing stage or during settlement
discussions is not a breach of the DFR. Id.
Here, you have not alleged any specific facts
supporting a DFR violation. Rather, it
appears that NJEA (and/or their affiliate)
represented you in a tenure arbitration
proceeding and obtained a favorable outcome.
The fact that NJEA (and/or its affiliate) did
not subsequently challenge the payroll
deductions from your back pay award is not,
by itself, a DFR violation. In fact, for the
reasons set forth above regarding subject
matter jurisdiction, NJEA (and/or its
affiliate) may have had a rational basis not
to pursue those claims.
Accordingly, pursuant to N.J.A.C.
19:14-2.3(a), your charge is dismissed in its
entirety and this case is closed. Any appeal
of this action must be filed within 10 days
of the above date in accordance with N.J.A.C.
19:14-2.3(b).
[Emphasis in original.]
C. White’s Appeal of the Director’s Decision
The instant appeal followed. In her January 24 appeal,
consisting of a three page email with no attachments, White

argues that the Director’s dismissal of her charge was in error.
She asserts that individual employees do have standing to pursue

charge met the pleading standard set forth in N.J.A.C. 19:14-

On January 27, the Commission’s Case Administrator notified
White that her January 24 appeal was deficient pursuant to
N.J.A.C. 19:14-2.3(b) because it was not “a self-contained

document enabling the Commission to rule on the basis of its
contents.” The deficiency letter instructed that White must
submit the record of documents that make up her case and provide

White was given a deadline of February 3. On that date, White
provided a 7-page email, reiterating her previous arguments from
her January 24 appeal, that included embedded download links,

D. The Parties’ Opposition to White’s Appeal.
On February 10, the Association filed its opposition to
White’s February 3 appeal. The Association argues that the
Director’s decision should be affirmed on procedural and
substantive grounds. The Association contends that White’s
appeal is procedurally deficient because her “email filled with
external links” was not properly served nor did it meet the
requirements of a “self-contained document” set forth in N.J.A.C.
19:14-2.3(b). Further, the Association asserts that the “facts”
and attachments White included in her February 3 email appeal

lists the 292 pages of attachments as follows: Original

January 22, 2026, My prior emails/appeal dated January 23-

Back-pay paystubs (“7 checks, Jan. 17, 2025"). White
states, “No other documents exist in the record.”
6/ White continued to send repetitive emails concerning her
appeal after February 3, 2026 that are not included as part
of the record.

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-41 11.
were not previously presented prior to her appeal of the
Director’s decision, and therefore, must not be considered. The
Association asserts the Director’s decision properly found that
White’s January 16 UPC was beyond the 6-month statute of
limitations. The Association further argues that the Director’s
decision should be affirmed because she fails to plead any
specific facts that establish that the Association represented
her in a manner that was arbitrary, discriminatory, or in bad
faith. Further, the Association argues that White’s requested
relief is beyond the jurisdiction of the Commission. The
Association asserts that White’s claims asserting violations of
Title 18A are properly the jurisdiction of the Commissioner of

deductions are properly the jurisdiction of the Department of

pension deductions are properly the jurisdiction of the Division
of Pensions.
On February 12, the Board filed its opposition to White’s
appeal of the Director’s decision. The Board asserts that White
has filed numerous complaints against the Board, regarding the
same allegations in the UPC, at the New Jersey Department of
Labor’s Wage and Hour Division and the New Jersey Department of
Education, and she has withdrawn each of the complaints. The
Board further argues the Director’s dismissal of the UPCs should

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-41 12.
be affirmed because the relief sought by the charges is outside
the authority of the Commission.
ANALYSIS
The Commission has authority to issue a complaint where it
appears that a charging party’s allegations, if true, may
constitute an unfair practice within the meaning of the Act.
N.J.S.A. 34:13A-5.4c; N.J.A.C. 19:14-2.1. We affirm the
Director’s decision to dismiss White’s UPC because she did not
plead sufficient facts to support the alleged violations of the
Act.7/
I. Charges Against the Board
White’s N.J.S.A. 34:13A-5.4a(5) charge against the Board
alleges “discrimination in employment terms to discourage union
membership, via targeted over-deductions.” The Director found
that individual employees do not have standing to pursue such a
charge because the employer’s duty to negotiate in good faith
only runs to the majority representative. New Jersey Tpk. Auth.
v. Beall, 1981 N.J. Super. Unpub. LEXIS 9 (App. Div. 1981),
aff’g, P.E.R.C. No. 81-64, 6 NJPER 560 (¶11284 1980); Sussex Cty.
Sheriff’s Office, P.E.R.C. No. 2021-49, 47 NJPER 527 (¶123 2021);
and Essex Cty. (Miller), P.E.R.C. No. 2019-16, 45 NJPER 195 (¶50
2018). We agree with the Director.
7/ As a threshold issue, we agree with the Director that
White’s filings do not demonstrate that they were timely
filed.

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-41 13.
Next, we turn to White’s N.J.S.A. 34:13A-5.4a(1) charge
against the Board, asserting its “interfer[ence] with union
rights by undermining NJEA dues and employee protections.”8/
White’s dispute against the Board stems from alleged improper
payroll deductions from a back pay award she obtained in a tenure
arbitration. In her February 3, 2026 appeal, she states, “I was
suspended on tenure charges; later, I obtained an
arbitration/back-pay award governed by N.J.S.A. 18A:6-14.”
(Emphasis added). In the attachments to her appeals, she
includes the tenure arbitrator’s award, which expressly states,
“I will retain jurisdiction of this matter to resolve any dispute
that arises as to the implementation of this award.” (Emphasis
added).
We agree with the Director that the record contains no
grounds for this agency to obtain jurisdiction over White’s
allegations concerning allegedly improper payroll deductions from
her back pay award. See State of New Jersey (Department of
Corrections and Youth Justice Commission, P.E.R.C. No. 2026-11,
52 NJPER 129 (¶33 2025)(dismissing an a(1) and (5) charge by an
individual employee against a public employer regarding disputed
pension calculations because this agency lacked jurisdiction over
such claims). Such jurisdiction may rest with the tenure
8/ We note that the January 21 second amended charge excludes
the a(3) charge which was raised in the January 16 amended
charge.

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-41 14.
arbitrator, the Commissioner of Education9/, the Department of
Labor and/or the Division of Pensions and Benefits.10/ Thus, the
Director correctly dismissed the N.J.S.A. 34:13A-5.4a(1) charge
against the Board.
III. Charge Against the Association
We next address White’s appeal of the Director’s dismissal
of her N.J.S.A. 34:13A-5.4b(1) charge against the Association,
alleging that it failed to file proposed grievances and ignored
her requests for assistance with the allegedly improper payroll
deductions.
In White’s January 16, 2026 first amended charge she states:
Beginning in 2025 and continuing thereafter,
I repeatedly sought assistance from my unions
(NJEA and EEA) regarding the improper
deduction and the Board’s refusal to correct
it. I filed grievances and sent multiple
emails, letters, and demands for action to
the NJEA/EEA and its assigned counsel . . . .
to no avail.
In White’s January 21 second amended charge she states that the
Association “[failed] to comply with grievance procedures or CBA
terms on payroll.”
9/ Pursuant to N.J.S.A. 18A:6-9, the Commissioner of Education
“shall have jurisdiction to hear and determine, without cost
to the parties, all controversies and disputes arising under
the school laws...”
10/ The Board asserts that White had complaints pending in other
venues but withdrew those complaints.

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-41 15.
N.J.S.A. 34:13A-5.4b(1) prohibits an employee organization
from “interfering with, restraining, or coercing employees in the
exercise of the rights guaranteed to them by the Act.” A breach
of the duty of fair representation violates subsection 5.4b(1) of
the Act and occurs when a union’s conduct towards a member of the
negotiations unit is arbitrary, discriminatory or in bad faith.
Lullo v. IAFF, 55 N.J. 409 (1970); D’Arrigo v. New Jersey State
Bd. of Mediation, 119 N.J. 74, 76 (1990); Belen v. Woodbridge Tp.
Bd. of Ed., 142 N.J. Super. 486 (App. Div. 1976); see also Vaca
v. Sipes, 386 U.S. 171 (1967).
A review of White’s emails about the alleged improper
payroll deductions demonstrates that they were largely directed
to the Board and its counsel, with multiple people copied
including Association representatives. The emails suggest that
White and the Board were involved in an appeal over payroll
deductions before the Department of Labor, and that she asked the
Association to provide her with different representation and
pursue grievances on her behalf.
The duty of fair representation does not require a union to
arbitrate every grievance. Essex Cty. (Miller), P.E.R.C. No.
2019-16, 45 NJPER 195 (¶50 2018); Passaic Cty. Support Staff
Ass’n, P.E.R.C. No. 2015-23, 41 NJPER 169 (¶60 2014). Unions are
provided wide latitude in determining whether a grievance is
meritorious and warrants action.11/ White’s emails show that the
11/ The Commission has frequently dismissed claims alleging that
(continued...)

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-41 16.
Association was on notice of both the Department of Labor appeal
and White’s dissatisfaction with her union representation.
However, given the discretion afforded unions in deciding whether
a grievance is meritorious, the emails do not establish that the
Association represented her in a manner that was arbitrary,
discriminatory or in bad faith. See Lullo v. IAFF, supra.
Thus, we affirm the Director’s decision dismissing White’s
N.J.S.A. 34:13A-5.4b(1) charge.
For all the foregoing reasons, we sustain the Director’s
January 22, 2026 decision dismissing White’s UPCs in their
entirety.
ORDER
The Charging Party’s appeal of the Director’s January 22,
2026 decision is denied.
BY ORDER OF THE COMMISSION
